title: Transactions
subtitle: Guaranteeing Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability via Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) and MVCC.
keyTakeaways: Atomicity and Durability are implemented at the storage layer using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) with redo and undo records.
Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) keeps multiple immutable versions of rows so readers never block writers and writers never block readers.
Long-running transactions hold open snapshots, preventing vacuuming/garbage collection and risking connection exhaustion.

sections.heading: 1. Architectural Fundamentals & Core Mechanics
sections.body: Databases do not flush modified 8KB data pages to disk on every `COMMIT` because random disk I/O is slow. Instead, they use the Write-Ahead Log (WAL) protocol: before any data page is modified, an append-only log record containing both Undo (old value) and Redo (new value) information is written sequentially to the WAL and flushed via `fsync`. Once the commit record hits the WAL on disk, the transaction is durable, even if power fails before dirty memory pages are checkpointed.
bullets: **Core Architectural Principle**: Atomicity and Durability are implemented at the storage layer using Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) with redo and undo records.
**Problem Space & Invariants**: Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) keeps multiple immutable versions of rows so readers never block writers and writers never block readers.
**System Boundary**: Operates across client network dispatch, gateway queuing, thread execution pools, and persistent storage I/O.

sections.heading: 2. Architectural Patterns & Implementation Topologies
sections.body: Distributed architectures apply specific implementation patterns and topologies for Transactions:
bullets: **Synchronous WAL Flush (fsync on every commit)**: Provides zero committed data loss on os crash or power failure (true acid durability). Best suited for Financial transactions, orders, user authentication, and core state.

**Asynchronous / Group Commit (`synchronous_commit = off`)**: Provides significantly higher write throughput by batching wal flushes every few milliseconds. Best suited for High-frequency analytics counters, audit logs, and non-critical telemetry.
Atomicity (Undo Log): If a transaction aborts or crashes mid-flight, the engine replays undo records backward to restore prior state.
Durability (Redo Log): Upon crash recovery, the engine replays committed WAL records forward from the last checkpoint.
Zero Read Locks: Readers see a consistent historical snapshot without acquiring shared locks that stall writers.
Dead Tuples & Vacuuming: Old row versions must be cleaned up asynchronously (`AUTOVACUUM` in Postgres or purge threads in InnoDB).

sections.heading: 3. Production Strengths: Where & How to Apply
sections.body: Production deployments apply Transactions across targeted operational scenarios:
bullets: **Where to Use: High-Impact Scenarios**: Optimal for Financial transactions, orders, user authentication, and core state, suited for environments requiring Zero committed data loss on OS crash or power failure (true ACID durability).

**Where to Use: High-Throughput Scenarios**: Recommended for High-frequency analytics counters, audit logs, and non-critical telemetry, where Significantly higher write throughput by batching WAL flushes every few milliseconds.

**How to Use: Engineering Implementation**: Instead of overwriting a row in place and locking out concurrent readers, MVCC stamps each tuple version with the creating transaction ID (`xmin` in Postgres) and deleting/updating transaction ID (`xmax`). Always establish explicit thresholds, measurement baselines, and automated monitoring.
**Architectural Leverage**: Provides predictable resource boundaries, bounds blast radius, and optimizes cost per transaction.

sections.heading: 4. Failure Modes & Trade-Offs: When to Avoid
sections.body: Improper implementation of Transactions introduces operational bottlenecks and failure modes:
bullets: **Where to Avoid: Trade-Off Bottlenecks**: Avoid when constraints cannot tolerate: commit latency is bounded by disk iops / nvme flush speed.
**Where to Avoid: Complexity Ceiling**: Avoid when operational requirements do not justify: up to a few milliseconds of committed transactions can be lost on sudden host failure.
**Catastrophic Failure Modes**: Uncalibrated parameters can trigger queue exhaustion, thread starvation, cascading retry storms, and tail latency amplification.
**Operational Overhead**: Requires continuous observability (p95/p99 latency tracking, saturation alerts, and distributed tracing across hop boundaries).

sections.heading: 5. Staff+ Engineering Verdict & Interview Playbook
sections.body: Technical guidelines and evaluation criteria for Transactions:
bullets: **Staff+ Golden Rule**: Long-running transactions hold open snapshots, preventing vacuuming/garbage collection and risking connection exhaustion.

**Staff+ Interview Playbook**: Always emphasize that external network calls (RPCs, payment gateways, message broker publishes) must never happen inside an open DB transaction block. Use an idempotency key or Transactional Outbox instead.
